title: Vowels & Length
intro:
Slovak vowels are pure and consistent — each one makes the same sound every time. The acute accent (dĺžeň) does not change the sound at all, it just holds the vowel about twice as long. Length changes meaning, so it matters: sud (barrel) vs súd (court).

One relief for English speakers: y and ý sound exactly the same as i and í. The difference is only spelling.

letters.sound: short 'a', like the a in father but clipped
long 'a' — the same vowel held about twice as long
short 'e', like the e in bed
long 'e' — the same vowel held about twice as long
short 'i', like the ee in see but clipped
long 'i' — the same vowel held about twice as long
sounds exactly like short i — the difference is only spelling
sounds exactly like long í — the difference is only spelling
short 'o', like the o in more but clipped

title: Č, Š, Ž, Dž
intro: The little hook (mäkčeň) turns four consonants into sounds English writes with two letters. Once you know these four, a huge share of Slovak spelling stops looking strange — they are the same sounds you already use in English, just written with one letter instead of two.

letters.sound: 'ch' as in chair
'sh' as in shoe
the 's' in measure or the g in genre
'j' as in jam

title: Soft Ď, Ť, Ň, Ľ
intro:
These are d, t, n and l said with the middle of the tongue pressed up against the roof of the mouth. English has close cousins inside words like 'due', 'tune', 'onion' and 'million'.

Important spelling rule: d, t, n and l are pronounced soft automatically before i, í and e in native Slovak words, even when no hook is written. So deti (children) sounds like ďeti.

letters.sound: soft d — close to the d in 'due'
soft t — close to the t in 'tune'
soft n — the ni in 'onion'
soft l — the lli in 'million'

title: Tricky Letters & Stress
intro:
Most remaining consonants work like English: b, d, f, g, k, l, m, n, p, s, t, v, z. (Q, W and X appear only in foreign words.) These are the ones that catch English speakers out.

Two rules worth memorising now:

1. Stress always falls on the first syllable of a word. No exceptions, no guessing.
2. R and L can act as vowels — a word can have no vowel letter at all and still be perfectly pronounceable: prst (finger), vlk (wolf), and the famous tongue-twister strč prst skrz krk.

letters.sound: 'ts' as in cats — never a k sound
'y' as in yes — never the English j
one single letter — raspy, like Scottish loch
'ds' as in roads
always pronounced, never silent
rolled/tapped with the tip of the tongue
a long syllabic r — the r itself is the vowel
a long syllabic l — the l itself is the vowel
